content: In 2020, approximately 10 million people developed tuberculosis (TB). A reduction in access to TB diagnostic and treatment services has led to an increase in TB-related deaths, with 1.5 million deaths reported in 2020 compared to 1.4 million in 2019. Among HIV-positive individuals, there were 214,000 additional TB-related deaths in 2020, up from 209,000 in 2019. This combined total of TB deaths has returned to levels observed in 2017. Between 2019 and 2020, there was a 15% reduction in the number of individuals receiving treatment for drug-resistant TB, decreasing from 177,100 to 150,359. This represents only about one-third of those in need of treatment. Additionally, there was a 22% decline in the detection of multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) cases, with 157,903 cases detected in 2020 compared to 201,997 in 2019. This decline aligns with an 18% reduction in the number of people newly diagnosed with TB and a 17% reduction in bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB cases during the same period. Globally, 150,359 individuals with MDR/RR-TB were enrolled in treatment in 2020, a 15% decrease from 177,100 in 2019. This level of enrollment corresponds to only about one in three people who develop MDR/RR-TB annually. However, treatment success rates have shown improvement. In 2018, the global treatment success rate for MDR/RR-TB was 59%, reflecting steady progress from 50% in 2012. The BPaLM regimen, a six-month treatment for MDR/RR-TB, was evaluated in the TB-PRACTECAL trial. This regimen includes bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, and moxifloxacin. It was compared to longer, more complex regimens, including 9–12-month injectable-containing regimens and 18–24-month WHO-recommended regimens. The BPaLM regimen demonstrated potential improvements in treatment success, reduced treatment failure, lower recurrence rates, and fewer adverse events. However, the evidence remains uncertain due to limitations in trial design, such as small sample sizes and lack of blinding. The BPaLM regimen offers significant advantages, including shorter treatment duration (six months compared to 9–24 months) and reduced pill burden. These factors are expected to improve patient adherence and reduce the workload on healthcare systems. The WHO panel judged the BPaLM regimen to have large desirable effects and minimal undesirable effects, despite the very low certainty of evidence. Cost analyses suggest that the BPaLM regimen is cost-saving compared to longer regimens, primarily due to reduced time in care, fewer outpatient visits, inpatient bed-days, and laboratory tests. The panel concluded that implementing the BPaLM regimen would likely lead to substantial cost savings and increased health equity, particularly in underserved and remote populations. The BPaLM regimen was also found to be acceptable to key stakeholders, including patients and healthcare providers, based on studies conducted in Indonesia, Kyrgyzstan, and Nigeria. Over 80% of participants rated the regimen as acceptable, citing its shorter duration and reduced complexity as key benefits. Feasibility studies indicated that 88% of stakeholders would likely implement the regimen once available. The WHO recommends the use of the six-month BPaLM regimen for patients with MDR/RR-TB, including those with fluoroquinolone resistance (pre-XDR-TB), as a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. This recommendation applies to adults and adolescents aged 14 years or older, regardless of HIV status, and excludes pregnant and breastfeeding women due to limited safety data on pretomanid. The recommended dose of linezolid in the BPaLM regimen is 600 mg daily. In summary, the BPaLM regimen represents a promising advancement in the treatment of drug-resistant TB, offering shorter treatment duration, improved outcomes, and cost savings.
